q: Where a switch controls a lighting load from a box, the grounded (neutral) conductor generally must be:
choices: Provided at the switch location (with listed exceptions)
explain: Electronic switches and occupancy sensors need a neutral; 404.2(C) requires one at most switch locations, with exceptions where conductors can be added later (e.g., raceway with enough room).

q: Switches and circuit breakers used as switches shall be installed so the center of the grip of the operating handle, in its highest position, is not more than how high above the floor or working platform?
explain: 6 ft 7 in. (2.0 m), same as the OCPD rule in 240.24(A). Exceptions for busways, hookstick-operated switches, and equipment-adjacent switches.

q: A grounding-type receptacle replaces a non-grounding receptacle where no equipment grounding conductor exists in the box. Which is a permitted option?
choices: Install a grounding-type receptacle and bond its ground screw to the neutral
Install a GFCI receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground'
explain: Options: another non-grounding receptacle; a GFCI-type receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground'; or a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI, marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground'. Never bond to the neutral.

q: A 15 or 20 A, 125 V receptacle installed outdoors in a wet location requires:
choices: A weatherproof cover that is weatherproof only when closed
An enclosure that is weatherproof whether or not a plug is inserted (in-use cover), with a listed weather-resistant receptacle
No cover if under a roof overhang
explain: Wet locations: in-use (bubble) cover plus a weather-resistant (WR) receptacle. Damp locations may use a cover weatherproof when closed.

q: In dwelling units, 15 and 20 A, 125 and 250 V receptacles in the areas specified in 210.52 generally must be:
explain: Tamper-resistant receptacles are required in dwellings (and in guest rooms, child-care facilities, etc.) with exceptions for receptacles above 5½ ft, dedicated appliance receptacles, and a few others.

q: The circuit directory of a panelboard must:
choices: List only the main breaker size
Legibly identify every circuit and modification for its clear, evident, and specific purpose
explain: Identification must be specific enough to distinguish circuits — 'lights' isn't enough; location and purpose are. Spare positions get labeled too.

q: A panelboard shall be protected on its supply side by an overcurrent device having a rating:
choices: Not greater than that of the panelboard
Of at least 125% of the panelboard rating
Equal to the feeder conductor ampacity only
explain: The panelboard's rating is the ceiling for the supply OCPD, with exceptions for panelboards fed from a protected transformer secondary and for existing 'lighting and appliance' panels.

q: In a clothes closet, a surface-mounted incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source must have at least what clearance from the nearest point of the storage space?
explain: Surface-mounted incandescent/LED enclosed: 12 in. Surface fluorescent and recessed enclosed incandescent/LED/fluorescent: 6 in. Luminaires identified for storage areas may be inside the storage space.

q: Cord-connected, chain-hung, or pendant luminaires and ceiling-suspended fans shall not be located within what zone around a bathtub rim or shower threshold?
explain: The bathtub/shower zone is 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the rim or threshold.

q: For a permanently connected appliance rated over 300 VA, the branch-circuit switch or circuit breaker may serve as the disconnect if it is:
choices: Within sight of the appliance or capable of being locked in the open position
Located in the same panel as the service
explain: Within sight, or lockable with the locking provision remaining in place whether or not the lock is installed.

q: A cord-and-plug-connected kitchen waste disposer's cord must be between:
explain: Disposer: 18–36 in. Built-in dishwasher or trash compactor: 3 ft to 6½ ft measured from the plug face to the plane of the appliance's rear.

q: When sizing branch-circuit conductors and short-circuit/ground-fault protection for a motor, the full-load current is taken from:
explain: Use the NEC tables for conductors, OCPD and disconnects; use the nameplate current for sizing overload protection (430.6(A)(2)).

q: A 10 hp, 230 V, three-phase motor (table FLC 28 A) requires branch-circuit conductors with an ampacity of at least:
explain: Single motor: 125% of table FLC = 28 × 1.25 = 35 A.

q: For the same 10 hp, 230 V, 3-phase motor (FLC 28 A), the maximum rating of an inverse-time circuit breaker for short-circuit and ground-fault protection is:
explain: Inverse-time breaker: 250% × 28 = 70 A (a standard size). Nontime-delay fuse 300%, dual-element time-delay fuse 175%, instantaneous-trip breaker 800%.

q: A continuous-duty motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 requires a separate overload device set at no more than what percentage of the nameplate full-load current?
explain: 125% for service factor 1.15 or more, or temperature rise 40°C or less; 115% for all other motors.

q: A disconnecting means for a motor must generally be located:
choices: Within sight of the motor location and driven machinery
explain: Within sight (visible and not more than 50 ft). The controller disconnect can serve if it is in sight of the motor, or with lockable provisions under the exception.

q: A motor-circuit disconnecting means must have an ampere rating of at least what percentage of the motor's full-load current?
explain: 115% of the table FLC, or an hp-rated switch of adequate rating.

q: Per Table 430.248, the full-load current of a 1 hp, 115 V, single-phase motor is:
explain: 115 V single-phase: ½ hp 9.8 A, ¾ hp 13.8 A, 1 hp 16 A, 1½ hp 20 A, 2 hp 24 A. At 230 V the values halve.

q: Branch-circuit conductors for a single hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor must have an ampacity of at least what percentage of the rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater?
explain: 125% — and the disconnect must be within sight and readily accessible (440.14).

q: A transformer rated 1000 V or less, protected on the primary side only, with a primary current of 9 A or more, requires a primary OCPD rated not more than:
explain: 125% of primary current (next standard size up permitted per Note 1). 2–9 A → 167%; less than 2 A → 300%.

q: A 1000 V-or-less transformer with primary-only protection has a primary current of 6 A. The maximum primary OCPD is:
explain: Primary currents from 2 to less than 9 A → 167%. Below 2 A → 300%.

q: A dry-type transformer rated 112½ kVA or less and 1000 V or less must generally have a separation of at least how much from combustible material (unless a barrier or complete enclosure is provided)?
explain: 12 in. (300 mm). Transformers over 112½ kVA need a transformer room of fire-resistant construction, with exceptions.

q: Per Table 430.250, the full-load current of a 5 hp, 208 V, three-phase motor is:
Receptacles installed in countertops or work surfaces:
choices: Shall not be installed in a face-up position unless listed for that purpose
explain: Face-up receptacles collect liquids and debris; only listed countertop assemblies are allowed.

q: Snap switches with metal faceplates shall be:
choices: Connected to an equipment grounding conductor (or protected by GFCI where no EGC exists)
explain: Metal yokes and faceplates must be effectively grounded; replacements without an EGC need GFCI protection or a nonmetallic, noncombustible faceplate.

q: A single non-motor-operated appliance is rated 20 A with no marked OCPD size. The branch-circuit overcurrent device shall not exceed:
explain: For appliances over 13.3 A with no marking, the OCPD can't exceed 150% of rated current: 20 × 1.5 = 30 A. Appliances rated 13.3 A or less: 20 A max.
